+## 4. How
+
+### Reclaim staleness check, after the fix
+
+```
+PROCEDURE reclaim_if_stale(identity, ownerSnapshot, env):
+  ref = spec.refName(identity)
+  existing = read_claim_manifest(ref)
+  IF existing is unreachable/missing/unreadable: (unchanged from today)
+
+  toleranceSecs = spec.applySkewTolerance === false ? 0 : resolveClaimClockSkewToleranceSecs(env)
+  skewedNowMs = current_time_ms() - toleranceSecs * 1000
+  held = spec.stalePredicate(existing.claim, skewedNowMs, env)
+  IF held: RETURN { reclaimed: false, reason: "held", holder: existing.claim, sha: existing.sha }
+
+  # everything below this line is UNCHANGED — the lease-matched CAS already fences
+  # the write against existing.sha, so a concurrent reclaimer or a revived holder
+  # (via confirmHead, on its own side) is already handled.
+  newClaim = spec.buildClaim(identity, ownerSnapshot, existing.claim.claim_epoch + 1)
+  push claim with `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<existing.sha>`
+  IF lease rejected: re-read, surface the new holder as "lease-lost"
+  ELSE: RETURN { reclaimed: true, sha: newCommitSha, claim: newClaim }
+```

+## 5. Design decision rationale
+
+**Margin-based tolerance vs. a holder-side monotonic counter.** The ticket names both as acceptable fix directions, with the counter marked "preferred." A counter that the reader can trust without comparing wall clocks would need the holder to write an always-advancing generation number the reader observes directly, which means changing what `claim.json` carries and how the heartbeat writer (`heartbeat.js`) updates it. The ticket's own scope section says the fix "does not change the claim wire shape." **`**Chosen:**` the margin-based tolerance** satisfies the scope constraint, needs no new field, and is a two-line change at a single call site.
+
+**Tolerance default: 60 seconds.** **`**Chosen:**` 60 seconds**, about 6.7 percent of the 900-second default heartbeat-stale window. Large enough to absorb realistic drift between two unsynchronized machines (NTP-synced hosts typically stay within a fraction of a second of each other; unmanaged clocks can drift by tens of seconds without correction), small enough that it barely delays reclaiming a genuinely crashed holder.
+
+**Env var name: `FAFF_CLAIM_CLOCK_SKEW_TOLERANCE_SECS`, no config-file key.** **`**Chosen:**` mirrors `FAFF_RUN_HEARTBEAT_STALE_SECS`**, which is also an env-only override with no `.faffrc.yaml` counterpart. Consistent with the existing pattern rather than introducing a new one. This override is also the escape hatch named in Failure modes for the "skew beyond the tolerance is unmitigated" case — an operator is never stuck with the 60-second default.
+
+**Per-predicate `applySkewTolerance` flag vs. a blanket call-site tolerance (round 2).** Round 1 of this spec applied `resolveClaimClockSkewToleranceSecs` unconditionally at the `reclaimIfStale` call site, to every binding's `stalePredicate` alike. The round-1 adversarial spec review's architectural lens objected: applying the tolerance without regard to whether a given predicate's reclaim decision carries any destructive blast radius is a straight, unnecessary delay wherever it doesn't buy safety, and the recovery path in particular pays that delay for no offsetting benefit. **`**Chosen:**` a per-binding `applySkewTolerance` flag, consumed at the `reclaimIfStale` call site, defaulting to `true`.** The default stays `true` (not `false`) deliberately: an unmodified `buildClaimStore` and a not-yet-shipped `landingClaimStore` both need to keep the tolerance, and a default of `true` means neither has to declare anything to get it — only the one binding that should NOT pay the delay (`recoveryClaimStore`) opts out explicitly. A default of `false` would have been the more dangerous direction: any binding that forgot to opt in would silently regain zero tolerance, quietly reopening exactly the wrong-direction risk (a live cross-box holder misjudged stale) this ticket exists to close.
+
+**`recoveryClaimStore` declares `applySkewTolerance: false` — zero added tolerance.** **`**Chosen:**` the recovery-claim reclaim path pays no delay beyond today's existing 900-second `heartbeatStaleSecs` window.** The reasoning does not depend on whether `recoveryClaimStore`'s underlying git-remote ref namespace can, in principle, be read from a different machine than wrote it — it can (the store's whole purpose, per its own header comment, is gating a "cross-box double-continue"). The reasoning instead turns on what a wrong verdict actually costs on this path versus the other two. On `buildClaimStore` and (once it ships) `landingClaimStore`, a reclaim that turns out to be wrong hands a build or a land to a second executor while the first is still actively, destructively working — the tolerance exists precisely to make that misjudgment rarer. On `recoveryClaimStore`, a reclaim that turns out to be wrong starts a *resume* of a stranded run segment a little early; per the WHY section's fail-safe principle, `confirmHead`'s CAS is unconditionally the actual backstop regardless of the tolerance, so the wrongly-reclaimed-from side's own `confirmHead` call refuses with `superseded` and it stops — the cost is one avoided-but-harmless resume attempt, not a double-drain, and the existing `hcReclaimB` fixture already exercises and accepts exactly this outcome as correct behaviour. Meanwhile a stranded segment sitting idle for an extra tolerance window before recovery even starts trying is a real, live cost with no corresponding safety upside on this path. Given that asymmetry — the tolerance buys real safety on the other two bindings and buys nothing on this one, while costing this one real recovery latency — zero tolerance is the better-tuned default for `recoveryClaimStore` specifically, independent of the same-box/cross-box framing either lens debates it in.
+
+**Recovery-claim reclaim timing is unchanged by this spec, so `hcReclaimB` needs no edit.** Round 1 chose to bump the fixture's baked heartbeat age from 2000ms to 90000ms to keep `hcReclaimB.reclaimed === true` passing once a blanket tolerance reached this predicate. Round 2's `applySkewTolerance: false` choice above removes the need for that edit outright: `recoveryClaimStore` never receives the tolerance, so the fixture's original 2-second baked age keeps working exactly as it did on `main`. **`**Chosen:**` leave the fixture's numbers untouched and add the regression-guard test described in HOW instead of an edit-and-reverify pair.** This is a stronger form of the same assurance the round-1 objection asked for (a test that would fail if the fixture were coincidentally green): rather than proving a new number works and the old number would now fail — which no longer applies, because the old number never stops working — the guard proves the `applySkewTolerance: false` wiring itself is load-bearing, by showing the identical scenario WOULD flip to "held" (fail to reclaim) if `recoveryClaimStore` inherited the default tolerance instead of opting out.
+
+**Problem 2: no logic change, coverage and documentation only.** **`**Chosen:**` after reading `reclaimIfStale`'s existing `--force-with-lease` fencing and the `pushX`/`pushY` selftest that already exercises it, the described TOCTOU window between two reclaimers is already closed.** The gap that remained was test coverage scoped to `recoveryClaimStore` only, and a comment that did not state the invariant explicitly enough to prevent this exact ticket. Both are additions, not corrections to broken logic. This conclusion is falsifiable by the new build-claims lease-race test; if it fails, the CAS is not what the code comments claim it is, and this rationale is wrong.
